subject: Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?

messages.author: 7d2a96af532ed7de
messages.subject: Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
parts:
Dear List,

Firstly, I can't imagine this hasn't come up before (although I couldn't find anything via search); advance apologies for any duplication!

I'm about to spend a daunting amount of time writing test procedures for various Stan models in R (which I should have done some time ago), using standardish 'test set', 'training set' methods.

What makes the process laborious (and easy to goof up!) is repeatedly re-writing code to mirror Stan model specifications in R, to generate (MC) predicted values for a new dataset (a la Gelman and Hill). The method outlined under 'Predictions as Generated Quantities' in the manual (p. 58) looks good, but is a little restrictive in that predictive MC simulations can only be run during a fit (as far as I've understood).

The predict.xxx (and Andrew's 'sim') functions in R make this a breeze, for the packages where they're available.

I can immediately think of lots of reasons why doing something similar for Stan would be tricky! But is it possible?

I get the impression it would best be done on the C++ side (flipping lp incrementing functions to rng counterparts), but could an R programmer (me) contribute anything useful?

Brendan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
parts:
Yes, it's come up, but this group's pretty much impossible
to search.

This is not meant to be an excuse for not having a built-in capability, but
one advantage of having to duplicate the effort outside Stan is that the testing
is more robust. If there's a mistake in the model, then just using
the broken model to generate test cases may not diagnose a problem.
It becomes a burden when you have to start lining up negative binomial
parameterizations --- bug again perhaps even more worth it for robustness.

To simulate in Stan, you need to take the model you built to
estimate, then rearrange declarations between data and parameters.
This will only work for continuous quantities. Alternatively you
can use the rng blocks as you suggest, but in that case, you have to
rewrite the code, as well. We can't just literally follow
the graphical model because there's never a graphical model declared
in Stan.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
parts: > Is it possible that the fixed_param sampler did not make it into the manual? Could not find it there.
It may have gotten lost when we split Stan and CmdStan.

> It sounds to me that this (although a bit tricky) is very close to what most people need as I can then use the stan model to generate mean-predictions which I then can in R "decorate" with a random number generator term if I need to simulate an observation. I "only" need to format the input data right.
>
> In short: With the fixed_param sampler the Stan program runs with the parameters I set for "initialization”?

Correct — the sampler will leave the parameters at their initial values (hence the name) and just call generated
quantities over and over again.

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
parts:
Hi Sebastian,

In the CmdStan manual, it's on pages 34 and 37.
It's mentioned in multiple places in the RStan manual.
PyStan also mentions it here: http://pystan.readthedocs.org/en/latest/api.html

But, it's not documented as well as it should be. What Micheal's mentioned is correct -- Stan initializes once and then uses that as fixed values of the parameters and continues.


Daniel

There's a section "Fixed Parameter Sampler" in the CmdStan manual

arguments in the interfaces because I think those vary. We want

fixed across the interfaces to the extent possible.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Is it possible to write a predict.stan type function?
parts:
The general manual is trying to steer clear of committing
to argument names, which is admittedly awkward.

"fixed_param" is what it's called in CmdStan. The manual avoids
using argument names from the interfaces, because they all use different
calling conventions.

Was it not clear how to call it from the CmdStan manual or was it
not clear what it did from the language manual?

The basic idea is that it runs a model without updating any
parameter values iteration to iteration. The usual use case is to
generate output using generated quantities. I'll make a note
to include an example of the kind of model you'd run this way in
the next version of the manual:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1081#issuecomment-60802573

- Bob

> On Oct 28, 2014, at 6:48 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I searched the user manual (not specific to any interface) for fixed_param, but did not find anything there.
>
> I did not find the "Sampling without Parameters" section, but this section is a bit disconnect (from my quick view on it) as I am left with question marks on how to do this then.
>
> On Monday, October 27, 2014 6:59:57 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Which manual are you talking about?
>
> There's a section "Fixed Parameter Sampler" in the CmdStan manual
> with the parameter fixed_param.
>
> There's a section called "Sampling without Parmeters" in the Stan
> manual itself, though it doesn't talk about the names of the
> arguments in the interfaces because I think those vary. We want
> to rationalize all of this when we move to Stan 3 so the names are
> fixed across the interfaces to the extent possible.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Oct 27, 2014, at 10:41 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Is it possible that the fixed_param sampler did not make it into the manual? Could not find it there. It sounds to me that this (although a bit tricky) is very close to what most people need as I can then use the stan model to generate mean-predictions which I then can in R "decorate" with a random number generator term if I need to simulate an observation. I "only" need to format the input data right.
> >
> > In short: With the fixed_param sampler the Stan program runs with the parameters I set for "initialization"?
> >
> > Sebastian
> >
> > On Monday, October 27, 2014 1:33:48 PM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > You can also use the fixed_param sampler, which will not update the parameters
> > (i.e. the model block is ignored) and just run the generated quantities.
> >
> > On Oct 27, 2014, at 4:04 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Yes, it's come up, but this group's pretty much impossible
> > > to search.
> > >
> > > This is not meant to be an excuse for not having a built-in capability, but
> > > one advantage of having to duplicate the effort outside Stan is that the testing
> > > is more robust. If there's a mistake in the model, then just using
> > > the broken model to generate test cases may not diagnose a problem.
> > > It becomes a burden when you have to start lining up negative binomial
> > > parameterizations --- bug again perhaps even more worth it for robustness.
> > >
> > > To simulate in Stan, you need to take the model you built to
> > > estimate, then rearrange declarations between data and parameters.
> > > This will only work for continuous quantities. Alternatively you
> > > can use the rng blocks as you suggest, but in that case, you have to
> > > rewrite the code, as well. We can't just literally follow
> > > the graphical model because there's never a graphical model declared
> > > in Stan.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >> On Oct 26, 2014, at 10:59 PM, Brendan <rocks....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >>
> > >> Dear List,
> > >>
> > >> Firstly, I can't imagine this hasn't come up before (although I couldn't find anything via search); advance apologies for any duplication!
> > >>
> > >> I'm about to spend a daunting amount of time writing test procedures for various Stan models in R (which I should have done some time ago), using standardish 'test set', 'training set' methods.
> > >>
> > >> What makes the process laborious (and easy to goof up!) is repeatedly re-writing code to mirror Stan model specifications in R, to generate (MC) predicted values for a new dataset (a la Gelman and Hill). The method outlined under 'Predictions as Generated Quantities' in the manual (p. 58) looks good, but is a little restrictive in that predictive MC simulations can only be run during a fit (as far as I've understood).
> > >>
> > >> The predict.xxx (and Andrew's 'sim') functions in R make this a breeze, for the packages where they're available.
> > >>
> > >> I can immediately think of lots of reasons why doing something similar for Stan would be tricky! But is it possible?
> > >>
> > >> I get the impression it would best be done on the C++ side (flipping lp incrementing functions to rng counterparts), but could an R programmer (me) contribute anything useful?
> > >>
> > >> Brendan
